characters: Sumaila: a thoughtful nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a royal-blue-and-yellow primary school uniform.
Madam Adwubi: his warm, encouraging Ghanaian class teacher wearing a sunflower-and-navy African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A quiet, nervous voice for Sumaila; a warm, clear teacher voice for Madam Adwubi
narrationPlan.pace: Hesitant at first, steady and brave after (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A soft, nervous tune that grows warm and bright (placeholder)
culturalNotes: In busy classrooms everywhere, shy learners sometimes nod along rather than risk embarrassment; a warm teacher response transforms classroom culture.
Sharing roasted groundnuts in equal piles connects fraction concepts directly to everyday Ghanaian school life.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Verify the numeracy: 8 shared equally into 2 groups gives 4 in each half.
Confirm that both pupil courage and warm, supportive teaching are portrayed positively.

teacherGuide.overview: An encouraging classroom story combining early fractions (finding half of an even set) with the confidence to speak up politely when something is unclear.
learningGoals: Find one half of an even group of objects by sharing equally into two.
Practise a polite classroom sentence for asking when unsure.
Explain how one learner’s brave question helps the whole class.
beforeReading: Ask: have you ever nodded in class even when a word or step still felt confusing?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 to praise Sumaila’s calm breath and polite hand-raising.
afterReading: Give pairs 8 bottle tops or pebbles to share equally into two groups and state: “Half of 8 is 4.”
Set up a welcoming “Curious Questions Box” where anyone can slip a question slip during the week.
discussion: What made asking feel scary for Sumaila at first?
How did Madam Adwubi’s smile make the whole room braver?
reflection: What polite words will you use the next time a lesson step feels unclear?

mathsExtension.task: Share 8 groundnuts equally between 2 friends. How many does each friend get?

support: Fold a paper circle cleanly into two matching halves and share 6 counters onto the two sides (3 and 3).
stretch: Find half of 12 and half of 20, and explain why 9 pebbles cannot be shared into two equal whole-pebble halves.

culturalNotes: In busy classrooms everywhere, shy learners sometimes nod along rather than risk embarrassment; a warm teacher response transforms classroom culture.
Sharing roasted groundnuts in equal piles connects fraction concepts directly to everyday Ghanaian school life.
localiseThis: Use bottle tops, smooth pebbles, or paper cutouts for hands-on equal sharing.
Establish a class agreement: we never laugh at a classmate’s honest question.
